task.situation: Every year, your town gives a ‘Young Citizen Award’ to a young person or group who has made life better for people in the area. Before the public vote, the youth page of the town’s website introduces the projects on this year’s shortlist. You have been asked to write about one of them.
task.instruction: Write an article in which you:
points: describe what the project does and how it started
explain what difference it makes to people in your area
suggest how readers can support it

words.short: Give your article a title. Write around 250 words.
words.long: Give your article a title. Write around 350 words.

task.de: Ein Artikel für die Jugendseite der Stadt-Website über ein Projekt, das für einen Jugendpreis nominiert ist. Drei Inhaltspunkte: beschreiben, was das Projekt macht und wie es begann; erklären, was es für die Menschen in der Gegend verändert; vorschlagen, wie Leser:innen es unterstützen können. Zuerst wählt ihr das Projekt, der Titel kommt ganz zum Schluss.

meta.publication: Town website · Youth page · Young Citizen Award shortlist

focus.label: relative clauses
focus.note: Marked: the relative pronoun or adverb that starts a relative clause (who, which, that, whose, where). After a comma, the clause is non-defining: it adds extra information and never starts with ‘that’.

gaps.q: Who started the project? Give our young hero ONE first name.
gaps.qDe: Ruft einen Vornamen für die Person, die das Projekt gestartet hat. Keine Namen von Mitschüler:innen oder Lehrer:innen.

gaps.q: How old is our hero now? Choose an age between 16 and 19.
gaps.qDe: Wie alt ist die Person heute? Ruft ein Alter zwischen 16 und 19.

steps.q: Which project on the shortlist do we write about?
steps.de: Wählt eines der drei erfundenen Projekte, über das unser Artikel berichtet.

options.label: Tech Tuesday
options.teaser: Every Tuesday, teenagers in the community centre help older people with phones, tablets and laptops.

options.label: Friday Kick-Off
options.teaser: Every Friday evening, teenagers run free football and basketball games for younger children in the park.

options.label: Reading Buddies
options.teaser: Twice a week, teenagers meet primary school children in the town library to read together.

steps.q: How do we open the article?
steps.de: Der erste Absatz führt die Leser:innen zu unserem Projekt. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then finish the introduction in your own words: make readers curious about our project.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann den Einstieg mit eigenen Worten fertigschreiben.

options.label: Ask the readers a question
options.why: A question speaks to readers directly and makes them think before the project appears.

map.tech: {{Have you ever tried to explain}} a video call to someone [[who]] has never used a smartphone? It can take a lot of patience. {{In our town, teenagers}} do exactly that once a week at Tech Tuesday, and older people love it.
map.sport: {{Where do you go when}} you are ten, it is Friday evening and there is nothing to do? For many children, the answer used to be ‘nowhere’. {{Thanks to the teenagers of Friday Kick-Off,}} they now have somewhere to run, play and meet friends [[who]] live nearby.
map.reading: {{Do you remember the first book [[that]] you read}} all on your own? For many children, reading is hard work [[that]] has nothing to do with fun. {{The teenagers of Reading Buddies}} want to change that, one story at a time.

options.label: Start with a scene
options.why: A short scene puts readers right into the place. They want to find out what is going on.

map.tech: {{It is a grey Tuesday afternoon, and}} the community centre is busy. At one table, a teenager is showing a pensioner how to send photos to her grandchildren. {{Welcome to Tech Tuesday,}} a free help desk [[where]] teenagers answer older people’s questions about phones and laptops.
map.sport: {{It is just after five on a Friday evening, and}} the park by the river is getting loud. Twenty children are chasing two footballs, while teenagers in orange shirts blow whistles. {{Welcome to Friday Kick-Off,}} a free sports evening [[that]] young people organise for local children.
map.reading: {{It is four o’clock on a Wednesday, and}} the children’s corner of the town library is unusually full. On every beanbag, a teenager and a six-year-old are sharing one book. {{Welcome to Reading Buddies,}} a project [[that]] brings older and younger readers together.

options.label: Start with a personal note

map.tech: Dear Editor, I am writing to you because I would like to tell your readers about a project in our town. It is called Tech Tuesday, and in my opinion it is the best project on the shortlist. I hope you will publish my text on the youth page.
map.sport: Dear Editor, I am writing to you because I would like to tell your readers about a project in our town. It is called Friday Kick-Off, and in my opinion it is the best project on the shortlist. I hope you will publish my text on the youth page.
map.reading: Dear Editor, I am writing to you because I would like to tell your readers about a project in our town. It is called Reading Buddies, and in my opinion it is the best project on the shortlist. I hope you will publish my text on the youth page.

options.reject: This is the start of a letter to the editor, not an article. An article has no ‘Dear Editor’, does not ask to be published and opens with a hook for its readers.
options.rejectDe: Das ist der Anfang eines Leserbriefs („Dear Editor“, Bitte um Veröffentlichung), kein Artikel. Ein Artikel beginnt mit einem Einstieg, der die Leser:innen packt.

steps.q: Content point 1: what does the project do, and how did it start?
steps.de: Erster Inhaltspunkt: was das Projekt macht und wie es begonnen hat. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then describe the project in your own words: who, where, when and what happens.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann das Projekt mit eigenen Worten beschreiben: wer, wo, wann, was passiert.

options.label: How it all started
options.why: Tells the start of the story in the past simple, then jumps to today. Readers see how a small idea grew.

map.tech: {{The idea for the project came from}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[who]] has always been good with technology. Two years ago, {NAME} noticed that many older neighbours were afraid of online forms and video calls. {{With the help of the community centre,}} {NAME} found a free room and three friends [[who]] wanted to join in. {{Today, Tech Tuesday opens}} its doors every week.
map.sport: {{The idea for the project came from}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[who]] has played football since primary school. Two years ago, {NAME} noticed that younger children had nowhere to play in the evenings, as the sports clubs had long waiting lists. {{With a ball and two friends,}} {NAME} started a weekly game in the park. {{Today, Friday Kick-Off attracts}} around forty children.
map.reading: {{The idea for the project came from}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[whose]] little brother found reading difficult at primary school. {NAME} spent a whole summer reading comics with him, and by September the boy was asking for more books. {{After that, {NAME} asked the library}} for a room and found five classmates [[who]] were happy to help. {{Today, Reading Buddies meets}} twice a week.

map.tech: {{The idea for the project came from}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[who]] has always been good with technology. Two years ago, {NAME} noticed that many older neighbours were afraid of online forms and video calls. {{With the help of the community centre,}} {NAME} found a free room and three friends [[who]] wanted to join in. {{Today, Tech Tuesday opens}} its doors every week. “Many older people think they are too old for technology,” {NAME} {{told us during our visit.}} “They just need someone [[who]] explains things slowly and never laughs at their questions.”
map.sport: {{The idea for the project came from}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[who]] has played football since primary school. Two years ago, {NAME} noticed that younger children had nowhere to play in the evenings, as the sports clubs had long waiting lists. {{With a ball and two friends,}} {NAME} started a weekly game in the park. {{Today, Friday Kick-Off attracts}} around forty children. “Football teaches you how to win and lose,” {NAME} {{told us during our visit.}} “But my favourite moment is when a shy child scores for the first time.”
map.reading: {{The idea for the project came from}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[whose]] little brother found reading difficult at primary school. {NAME} spent a whole summer reading comics with him, and by September the boy was asking for more books. {{After that, {NAME} asked the library}} for a room and found five classmates [[who]] were happy to help. {{Today, Reading Buddies meets}} twice a week. “Some children are sure they are bad at reading,” {NAME} {{told us during our visit.}} “But once they find a story [[that]] they really like, they want to know what happens next.”

options.label: What happens there
options.why: Describes the project in the present simple with concrete examples, so readers can picture it.

map.tech: {{The project was started two years ago by}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[whose]] grandfather once needed a whole afternoon to buy a train ticket online. Anyone over sixty can bring a phone, tablet or laptop to Tech Tuesday. {{The volunteers explain}} video calls or online forms step by step. {{Questions [[that]] seem silly}} are welcome, and nobody is in a hurry.
map.sport: {{The project was started two years ago by}} {NAME}, {AGE}, a keen footballer [[who]] saw bored children in the park. Every Friday from five to seven, children aged eight to twelve can play football for free at Friday Kick-Off. {{The teenagers bring the balls,}} plan games and make sure that everybody plays, even children [[who]] have never been in a team.
map.reading: {{The project was started two years ago by}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[who]] wanted more children to enjoy books. At Reading Buddies, each teenager meets the same younger child at the library twice a week. {{Together they choose a book,}} read it aloud in turns and talk about the story. {{The children, [[who]] are between six and nine,}} can then take the books home.

map.tech: {{The project was started two years ago by}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[whose]] grandfather once needed a whole afternoon to buy a train ticket online. Anyone over sixty can bring a phone, tablet or laptop to Tech Tuesday. {{The volunteers explain}} video calls or online forms step by step. {{Questions [[that]] seem silly}} are welcome, and nobody is in a hurry. {{At first, however, hardly anyone came,}} as many older people did not trust strangers with their bank details. {{The team solved this with one clear rule:}} volunteers never type in passwords. These days, there is often a queue at the door.
map.sport: {{The project was started two years ago by}} {NAME}, {AGE}, a keen footballer [[who]] saw bored children in the park. Every Friday from five to seven, children aged eight to twelve can play football for free at Friday Kick-Off. {{The teenagers bring the balls,}} plan games and make sure that everybody plays, even children [[who]] have never been in a team. {{In the first winter, however, it was}} too dark and cold to play outside. {{The team solved this by asking}} a local school, [[which]] now lets them use its gym from November to March.
map.reading: {{The project was started two years ago by}} {NAME}, {AGE}, [[who]] wanted more children to enjoy books. At Reading Buddies, each teenager meets the same younger child at the library twice a week. {{Together they choose a book,}} read it aloud in turns and talk about the story. {{The children, [[who]] are between six and nine,}} can then take the books home. {{At first, however, some children came only once.}} {{The team solved this by asking}} them what they wanted to read: comics, animal facts and funny stories. The library bought a box of them, and now hardly anyone misses a meeting.

steps.ownLong: Copy the frame. Then describe in your own words who started the project, what happens there and how it got going. Add one quote or one problem the team solved.
steps.ownLongDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann mit eigenen Worten beschreiben, wer das Projekt gestartet hat, was dort passiert und wie es angelaufen ist; dazu ein Zitat oder eine Hürde, die das Team gelöst hat.

steps.q: Content point 2: what difference does the project make?
steps.de: Zweiter Inhaltspunkt: was das Projekt für die Menschen in der Gegend verändert. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then explain in your own words what difference the project makes and give one example.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann mit eigenen Worten erklären, was das Projekt verändert, und ein Beispiel geben.

options.label: People meet
options.why: Focuses on the community: people meet who would not meet otherwise. Relative clauses add the details.

map.tech: {{Apart from fixing phones, Tech Tuesday brings two generations together.}} Pensioners [[who]] live on their own get company and a reason to leave the house. {{At the same time, teenagers hear}} stories about life before the internet, [[which]] many of them find fascinating. {{In a town [[where]] generations rarely meet,}} contact like this is worth a lot.
map.sport: {{Apart from the games, Friday Kick-Off brings}} children and families from the whole area together. Boys and girls from different schools and backgrounds play in the same team, and parents get to know each other at the side of the pitch. {{For families [[who]] cannot afford club fees,}} the project is a real gift.
map.reading: {{Apart from teaching reading, the project creates friendships across age groups.}} The younger children get a role model [[who]] is neither a parent nor a teacher, and they look up to their buddies. {{The teenagers, in turn, feel}} needed and take their job very seriously. {{Some pairs [[that]] met in the first year}} still read together every week.

map.tech: {{Apart from fixing phones, Tech Tuesday brings two generations together.}} Pensioners [[who]] live on their own get company and a reason to leave the house. {{At the same time, teenagers hear}} stories about life before the internet, [[which]] many of them find fascinating. {{In a town [[where]] generations rarely meet,}} contact like this is worth a lot. {{An 82-year-old visitor, for example,}} used to spend Tuesdays alone at home; now he looks forward to it all week, and the young people even ask him for advice.
map.sport: {{Apart from the games, Friday Kick-Off brings}} children and families from the whole area together. Boys and girls from different schools and backgrounds play in the same team, and parents get to know each other at the side of the pitch. {{For families [[who]] cannot afford club fees,}} the project is a real gift. {{A mother [[whose]] two sons come every week}} says that her boys used to sit on the sofa all weekend; now they have friends from all over the neighbourhood, and so does she.
map.reading: {{Apart from teaching reading, the project creates friendships across age groups.}} The younger children get a role model [[who]] is neither a parent nor a teacher, and they look up to their buddies. {{The teenagers, in turn, feel}} needed and take their job very seriously. {{Some pairs [[that]] met in the first year}} still read together every week. {{One father says that his daughter}} talks about her buddy all the time and that the library has become her favourite place in town.

options.label: Good for everybody

map.tech: Tech Tuesday is very important for our town because it helps people which have problems with technology. Everything what the volunteers explain is useful in everyday life, and the visitors, that come every week, have become real friends of the team. Some of them even bring cake for everyone now, and others tell all their friends about the project.
map.sport: Friday Kick-Off is very important for our area because it helps children which have nowhere to play. Everything what they learn on the pitch is useful in everyday life, and the parents, that come to watch, have become real friends of the team. Some of them even bring drinks for everyone now, and a few have started to help with the games.
map.reading: Reading Buddies is very important for our town because it helps children which find reading difficult. Everything what they read with their buddies makes them more confident, and the parents, that pick them up, have become real friends of the team. Some of them even bring cake for everyone now, and a few help to tidy up the book corner.

options.reject: Three typical mistakes with relative clauses: ‘which’ for people (→ who), ‘everything what’ (→ everything that) and ‘that’ after a comma (→ who, with no commas).
options.rejectDe: Drei typische Fehler bei Relativsätzen: which für Personen → who, everything what → everything that, that nach einem Beistrich → who ohne Beistriche.

map.tech: Tech Tuesday is very important for our town because it helps people which have problems with technology. Everything what the volunteers explain is useful in everyday life, and the visitors, that come every week, have become real friends of the team. Some of them even bring cake for everyone now, and others tell all their friends about the project. An 82-year-old man can now make video calls to his granddaughter in Canada on his own. Before his first visit, he was always afraid of pressing the wrong button, so he never tried.
map.sport: Friday Kick-Off is very important for our area because it helps children which have nowhere to play. Everything what they learn on the pitch is useful in everyday life, and the parents, that come to watch, have become real friends of the team. Some of them even bring drinks for everyone now, and a few have started to help with the games. One mother says that her two sons used to sit on the sofa all weekend. Now they count the days until Friday and have made friends from all over the neighbourhood.
map.reading: Reading Buddies is very important for our town because it helps children which find reading difficult. Everything what they read with their buddies makes them more confident, and the parents, that pick them up, have become real friends of the team. Some of them even bring cake for everyone now, and a few help to tidy up the book corner. A primary school teacher has noticed the change in her class. Pupils who used to hide behind their books now put up their hands to read aloud.

options.label: People grow
options.why: Focuses on what people gain, from independence to new skills, and makes the benefit concrete.

map.tech: {{For older people, Tech Tuesday means more than a working phone: it helps them to stay independent.}} More and more everyday tasks, such as booking a doctor’s appointment, only work online. {{People [[who]] cannot do this}} often have to wait for help from their families. {{After a few Tuesdays at the centre,}} many visitors manage on their own.
map.sport: {{For the children, Friday Kick-Off is more than a game: it keeps them active.}} Many of them spend hours in front of screens, [[which]] is not good for their health. {{On Friday evenings, they}} run around for two hours and learn to play fairly. {{The teenagers [[who]] lead the games}} learn a lot, too, from planning to staying calm.
map.reading: {{For the children, Reading Buddies is more than a story: it helps them to become better readers.}} Reading is the key to almost every school subject, and children [[who]] read for fun usually find school easier. {{In a relaxed setting [[where]] nobody gives marks,}} they lose their fear of making mistakes. {{Many of them have started borrowing}} books on their own.

map.tech: {{For older people, Tech Tuesday means more than a working phone: it helps them to stay independent.}} More and more everyday tasks, such as booking a doctor’s appointment, only work online. {{People [[who]] cannot do this}} often have to wait for help from their families. {{After a few Tuesdays at the centre,}} many visitors manage on their own. One woman, for example, had never written an email before her first visit. Three months later, she booked her own flu jab online and showed her neighbour how to do it.
map.sport: {{For the children, Friday Kick-Off is more than a game: it keeps them active.}} Many of them spend hours in front of screens, [[which]] is not good for their health. {{On Friday evenings, they}} run around for two hours and learn to play fairly. {{The teenagers [[who]] lead the games}} learn a lot, too, from planning to staying calm. Some children have even found their way into a real team: last season, six of them joined football clubs in town, [[where]] they now train twice a week.
map.reading: {{For the children, Reading Buddies is more than a story: it helps them to become better readers.}} Reading is the key to almost every school subject, and children [[who]] read for fun usually find school easier. {{In a relaxed setting [[where]] nobody gives marks,}} they lose their fear of making mistakes. {{Many of them have started borrowing}} books on their own. A primary school teacher has noticed the change: “Some of my pupils used to hide behind their books. Now they put up their hands to read aloud.”

steps.ownLongDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann mit eigenen Worten erklären, was das Projekt verändert, und ein Beispiel für eine Person geben, der es geholfen hat.

steps.q: Content point 3: how can readers support the project?
steps.de: Dritter Inhaltspunkt: wie Leser:innen das Projekt unterstützen können. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.

steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann eigene Ideen ergänzen, wie Leser:innen helfen können, und begründen.

options.label: Appeal to the readers

map.tech: Tech Tuesday is simply the most amazing, wonderful and fantastic project in the whole world, and anybody who does not support it should be ashamed of themselves. Please, please, please help these incredible heroes! They are the kindest, bravest and most generous people anyone has ever met. Believe me, if you do nothing, you will regret it forever!
map.sport: Friday Kick-Off is simply the most amazing, wonderful and fantastic project in the whole world, and anybody who does not support it should be ashamed of themselves. map.reading: Reading Buddies is simply the most amazing, wonderful and fantastic project in the whole world, and anybody who does not support it should be ashamed of themselves. Please, please, please help these incredible heroes! They are the kindest, bravest and most generous people anyone has ever met. Believe me, if you do nothing, you will regret it forever!

options.reject: Far too emotional and pushy for an article: ‘the most amazing … in the whole world’, ‘should be ashamed of themselves’, ‘please, please, please’. An article persuades with concrete tips and reasons, not with exaggeration and pressure.
options.rejectDe: Viel zu emotional und aufdringlich für einen Artikel (the most amazing … in the whole world, should be ashamed of themselves, please, please, please): Ein Artikel überzeugt mit konkreten Tipps und Gründen, nicht mit Übertreibung und Druck.

options.label: Join the team
options.why: Gives readers three concrete ways to take part, so that everyone can find one that suits them.

map.tech: {{A project like this needs support.}} {{The easiest way to help is to}} tell older relatives or neighbours [[who]] struggle with technology about Tech Tuesday. {{Why not join as a volunteer?}} You do not need to be an expert, just patient and friendly. {{Finally,}} you could give the team old phones [[that]] you no longer use.
map.sport: {{A project like this needs support.}} {{One way to help is to}} come along on a Friday and help with the games, as no coaching experience is needed. {{Why not donate}} sports equipment [[that]] is lying around at home, such as balls, cones or football shirts? {{Finally,}} tell families with younger children about the project.
map.reading: {{A project like this needs support.}} {{One way to help is to}} become a reading buddy yourself: you only need two hours a week, and the team shows newcomers everything. {{Why not give}} children’s books [[that]] you no longer read to the library? {{Finally,}} tell families with young children about Reading Buddies.

map.tech: {{A project like this needs support.}} {{The easiest way to help is to}} tell older relatives or neighbours [[who]] struggle with technology about Tech Tuesday. {{A personal tip from someone they trust}} often works better than a poster. {{Why not join as a volunteer?}} You do not need to be an expert, just patient and friendly, and the team shows every newcomer the ropes. {{Finally,}} you could give the team old phones [[that]] you no longer use, so that visitors can practise without being afraid of breaking anything.
map.sport: {{A project like this needs support.}} {{One way to help is to}} come along on a Friday and help with the games, as no coaching experience is needed. {{Even one evening a month helps}} when forty children turn up. {{Why not donate}} sports equipment [[that]] is lying around at home, such as balls, cones or football shirts? A bag of old shirts can quickly become a set of team colours. {{Finally,}} tell families with younger children about the project, especially families [[who]] have just moved to the area.
map.reading: {{A project like this needs support.}} {{One way to help is to}} become a reading buddy yourself: you only need two hours a week, and the team shows newcomers everything. {{What matters most is patience,}} not a love of long novels. {{Why not give}} children’s books [[that]] you no longer read to the library? {{Picture books in good condition}} are always welcome. {{Finally,}} tell families with young children about Reading Buddies, as many parents still do not know that the project exists.

options.label: Small steps for everyone
options.why: Shows that everybody can help, even without much time. The examples make the tips easy to follow.

map.tech: {{Even readers [[who]] cannot come along can help a project like this.}} For instance, you can follow Tech Tuesday online and share its posts. {{Why not start at home?}} Show a grandparent one new thing on their phone this week. {{Better still,}} you could help neighbours [[who]] find online forms confusing.
map.sport: {{Even readers [[who]] cannot come along can help a project like this.}} For instance, you can follow Friday Kick-Off online and share its posts. {{Why not ask}} a younger brother, sister or neighbour [[who]] is bored on Friday evenings to join in? {{Better still,}} you could start a similar game in a park near you.
map.reading: {{Even readers [[who]] cannot come along can help a project like this.}} For instance, you can follow Reading Buddies online and share its posts. {{Why not read}} a story to a younger brother, sister or cousin this week? {{Better still,}} you could start a reading corner at your own school, [[where]] older students read with younger ones.

map.tech: {{Even readers [[who]] cannot come along can help a project like this.}} For instance, you can follow Tech Tuesday online and share its posts, so that more families hear about it. {{Why not start at home?}} Show a grandparent one new thing on their phone this week, such as how to make the letters bigger. {{It only takes five minutes,}} and it can save them a lot of stress. {{Better still,}} you could help neighbours [[who]] find online forms confusing. Small steps like these are exactly what the project is about.
map.sport: {{Even readers [[who]] cannot come along can help a project like this.}} For instance, you can follow Friday Kick-Off online and share its posts, so that more families hear about it. {{Why not ask}} a younger brother, sister or neighbour [[who]] is bored on Friday evenings to join in? {{Shy children find it easier to take part}} when they already know someone there. {{Better still,}} you could start a similar game in a park near you. All you need is a ball, a free evening and a few friends.
map.reading: {{Even readers [[who]] cannot come along can help a project like this.}} For instance, you can follow Reading Buddies online and share its posts, so that more families hear about it. {{Why not read}} a story to a younger brother, sister or cousin this week? {{Ten minutes at bedtime are enough,}} and small children love hearing the same story again and again. {{Better still,}} you could start a reading corner at your own school, [[where]] older students read with younger ones once a week.

steps.de: Der Schluss rundet den Artikel ab. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.

steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann die Sätze mit eigenen Worten fertigschreiben: eine klare Botschaft an die Leser:innen.

options.label: Sum it up
options.why: Sums up the message of the article and links back to the award.
options.text: {{All in all, you do not have to be famous to be a hero.}} {NAME} and the team show that one small idea can change a whole neighbourhood. {{When you vote for this year’s Young Citizen Award,}} remember this project, [[which]] deserves our votes and our support.

options.label: Challenge the readers
options.why: Speaks to readers directly and leaves them with a question to think about.
options.text: {{Next time you think one person cannot change anything, remember {NAME}.}} Big projects start with someone [[who]] dares to try a small idea, and they grow when others join in. {{So look around your neighbourhood:}} what is missing? Maybe next year’s Young Citizen Award will go to you.

steps.q: Now that the article is finished, which title do we choose?
steps.de: Der Titel kommt zuletzt und soll neugierig machen und zum Inhalt passen.
steps.own: Short and catchy: make readers curious about our project.
steps.ownDe: Kurz und treffend: Der Titel soll neugierig auf unser Projekt machen.

options.label: A short slogan
options.why: Short and catchy, and it already contains the message of the article.

map.tech: Never too old to go online
map.sport: Every Friday, everybody plays
map.reading: Big readers, little readers

options.label: A question
options.why: A question in the title makes readers curious about the answer.

map.tech: Can you teach Grandpa to make a video call?
map.sport: What happens in the park on Friday evenings?
map.reading: Who’s afraid of a thick book?

options.label: Name the heroes
options.why: Says who the article is about, and the relative clause tells us what they do.

map.tech: The teenagers [[who]] keep older people online
map.sport: The teenagers [[who]] made Friday the best day of the week
map.reading: The teenagers [[who]] turn children into readers

options.label: Name the award
options.text: Why we need the Young Citizen Award
options.reject: This title is about the award, not about our project: readers would expect an article on why the town needs the prize. A title has to say what the article is really about.
options.rejectDe: Der Titel handelt vom Preis, nicht von unserem Projekt: Leser:innen erwarten einen Artikel darüber, warum die Stadt den Preis braucht. Der Titel muss zum Inhalt passen.

checks.en: A title that makes readers curious
An introduction with a hook (question or scene)
All three content points: what the project does and how it started, the difference it makes, how readers can support it
Five paragraphs: each body paragraph opens with a clear link to the one before
Relative clauses with who, which, that, whose and where add information
Non-defining relative clauses stand between commas and never start with ‘that’
Neutral, friendly register: no chat slang

teacher.aim: Die Klasse baut gemeinsam einen B1-Artikel über ein erfundenes Jugendprojekt, das für einen Preis der Stadt nominiert ist, und übt dabei Einstieg, Topic Sentences, Register und vor allem Relativsätze (defining und non-defining, who, which, that, whose, where).
teacher.prep: A/B/C/D-Karten austeilen (eine Garnitur pro Person). Beamer im Vollbild. Die Aufgabe am Beamer enthält alles Nötige. Die Klasse sollte Relativsätze schon kennen; kurz an den Unterschied erinnern: ohne Beistriche = notwendige Information (that möglich), mit Beistrichen = Zusatzinformation (nie that). Im Gerüst-Modus den eingebauten Timer nutzen: 5 min pro Absatz, bei Bedarf +1.
teacher.heft: Neue Seite: Datum rechts oben, darunter „Article“ als Überschrift (wie am Beamer). Dann 2 Zeilen für den Titel frei lassen, der Titel kommt zuletzt. Jeder der fünf Absätze beginnt nach einer Leerzeile, am Rand steht das Kurzwort: Intro, Body 1, Body 2, Body 3, Conclusion. Relativpronomen grün unterstreichen, bei non-defining Relativsätzen auch die Beistriche einkreisen.
teacher.flow: 7 Entscheidungen: Projekt, fünf Absätze (jede Entscheidung ist ein ganzer Absatz), Titel. Volltext kurz (50 min): 5 min Aufgabe lesen und Projekt wählen, 6 weitere Entscheidungen à ca. 2 min, Abschreiben ca. 20 min, 5 min Checkliste. Volltext lang (Doppelstunde): dieselben 7 Entscheidungen, aber die drei Body paragraphs sind länger, daher ca. 30–35 min Abschreiben; die restliche Zeit für die Besprechung der Fallen und den Beginn der Hausübung nutzen. Gerüst kurz (realistisch ca. 60 min): 5 min Aufgabe und Projekt; pro Absatz 1 min Entscheidung, 5–6 min eigenes Schreiben, 1 min Vergleich mit dem Modell; am Ende 5 min Checkliste. In einer 50-Minuten-Stunde den Schluss noch abstimmen und das Gerüst abschreiben lassen; Schluss fertigschreiben und eigenen Titel finden als Hausübung. Nach der Abstimmung in Body 1 die wichtigsten Fakten zum Projekt (Name, Ort, Wochentag) kurz an die Tafel schreiben. Gerüst lang: Doppelstunde (100 min), gleicher Rhythmus, für jeden Body paragraph 7–8 min eigenes Schreiben, dazwischen eine Vergleichsrunde zu zweit.
teacher.traps: Introduction C (TA): Textsorte verfehlt, Anfang eines Leserbriefs („Dear Editor“, Bitte um Veröffentlichung) statt eines Artikels. Body 2 B (LSA): which für Personen, everything what, that nach einem Beistrich. Body 3 A (LSR): viel zu emotional und aufdringlich (the most amazing … in the whole world, should be ashamed of themselves, please, please, please): Übertreibung und Druck statt konkreter Tipps und Gründe. Title D (TA): Der Titel handelt vom Preis, nicht von unserem Projekt, und passt nicht zum Inhalt. Kürzel: TA = Erfüllung der Aufgabenstellung, CC = Kohärenz und Kohäsion, LSR = Spektrum sprachlicher Mittel, LSA = Sprachrichtigkeit.
teacher.notes: Der Artikel hat in beiden Längen genau fünf Absätze (Intro, drei Body paragraphs mit je einem Inhaltspunkt, Conclusion). Die lange Fassung hat dieselben Entscheidungen; die drei Body paragraphs sind länger (ein Zitat, eine Hürde vom Anfang, ein konkretes Beispiel, Gründe für jeden Tipp), Einleitung und Schluss bleiben gleich. Die drei Projekte und der Jugendpreis sind erfunden. Die Person, die das Projekt gestartet hat, bekommt von der Klasse einen Vornamen und ein Alter (16–19): nur erfundene Namen, keine Namen von Mitschüler:innen oder Lehrer:innen. Der Text kommt bei dieser Person ohne er/sie aus, daher passt jeder Name. Die Falle in Body 2 eignet sich gut für eine kurze Wiederholung der Relativpronomen an der Tafel. Differenzierung: Schnelle schreiben im Gerüst-Modus pro Absatz einen zusätzlichen Satz mit einem non-defining Relativsatz. Hausübung: denselben Artikel über ein echtes Projekt in der eigenen Umgebung oder eine zweite Fassung mit einem anderen Projekt.
